mcqs.question: A SwiftUI View is a struct whose body is recomputed frequently. Where does data that must survive across those recomputations actually live?
options: It doesn't survive — every recomputation starts from scratch by design
As a plain stored property on the struct itself
In a global singleton the view reads from
In storage SwiftUI manages outside the struct's own lifetime, accessed via a property wrapper like @State
mcqs.explanation: Because the struct itself is disposable and recreated on every relevant update, @State's actual storage lives outside the struct, managed by SwiftUI, so the value persists across body being recomputed. A plain property would reset every time the struct is recreated.

mcqs.question: Two sibling views both declare their own @State for what is supposed to be the same toggle value. What's the resulting bug?
options: The two views silently drift out of sync because each owns an independent copy of the state
A compile error, since SwiftUI disallows duplicate @State names
SwiftUI automatically merges the two into a shared binding
Only the first view's @State actually takes effect at runtime
mcqs.explanation: Each @State is its own independent storage; there is no automatic merging, so two views each holding their own state for the same logical value can diverge the moment one changes without the other. The fix is a single owner using @State, with every other view getting a @Binding to it.

mcqs.question: A ForEach loop renders list rows without a stable, unique id per element. What breaks when the underlying array is reordered?
options: The app crashes at runtime because ForEach requires Identifiable
SwiftUI treats the reordered rows as destroyed-and-recreated views rather than moved ones, breaking animations and per-row state
Nothing breaks — SwiftUI always tracks array elements by their original index automatically
Only the visual order changes; row-level @State is unaffected
mcqs.explanation: Without a stable identity, SwiftUI can't tell that a row simply moved rather than being a new element at that position, so it treats it as a fresh view — animations snap instead of sliding, and any per-row @State resets. ForEach doesn't require Identifiable if you supply an id key path explicitly, and this doesn't crash.

mcqs.question: A team is building a brand-new screen with no legacy UIKit dependencies. What's the strongest reason to default to SwiftUI over UIKit here?
options: SwiftUI has more mature support for custom scroll physics and complex gestures
UIKit is deprecated and no longer receives updates
Less boilerplate for a standard screen, with easier previews and stronger accessibility defaults, and no legacy constraint forcing UIKit
SwiftUI cannot interoperate with UIKit, so mixing frameworks is impossible
mcqs.explanation: For a genuinely new screen, SwiftUI's lower boilerplate and built-in accessibility usually win when there's no legacy constraint pulling toward UIKit. UIKit is not deprecated, interop via UIViewRepresentable is very much possible, and UIKit is still the more mature choice specifically for complex custom gestures and scroll physics.

mcqs.question: A background task fetches data and directly assigns the result to a @State property without hopping back to the main actor. What's the risk?
options: The @State value will update the UI but with a one-frame delay
The app will always crash immediately with a concurrency error
None — @State is thread-safe by design and updates correctly from any thread
The mutation may not reliably land on the view as expected, since UI state is meant to be touched on the main actor
mcqs.explanation: SwiftUI's state and rendering are designed around main-actor isolation; mutating from off the main actor risks updates not landing correctly, and stricter Swift concurrency checking flags or blocks it rather than silently working. It's not guaranteed to crash, and it's not simply a one-frame delay — the outcome is unreliable, which is the actual problem.
